title: Teaching
text:
Topics in Development Economics (EC310), 2025-26 Course page


Course content

This module looks at a range of economic problems in low-income countries. It shows how the tools of economic analysis, especially models of household behaviour, can explain economic behaviour and help design policies to address acute economic problems. Topics may include agricultural households, the behavioural aspects of poverty, culture, child labour, comparative development, the determinants of growth, education, firms, gender, health, institutions, labour markets, market failures and microfinance, poverty and inequality, and policy on issues such as migration and industrialisation.

title: Teaching
text:
London School of Economics

Microeconomic Principles I (EC201), 2020-21


Course content

This is an intermediate course in microeconomic analysis. It gives a broad overview of economic principles, including some recent developments in thinking, and teaches students to apply the tools of microeconomics to concrete economic problems. The course starts with consumer theory, covering preferences and utility, demand, income and substitution effects and welfare analysis, with applications to savings and labour supply. It then moves on to behavioural economics and decision-making under risk, including expected utility, insurance and prospect theory. Producer theory covers production and cost functions, supply and market structure, and game theory is applied to oligopoly and auctions. Later topics include general equilibrium, efficiency and inequality, public goods and externalities, political economy, contracts under moral hazard and adverse selection, and innovation, along with the role of government in each.



Economics B (EC102), 2019-20


Course content

This is an introductory course in microeconomics and macroeconomics. The first half covers consumer and producer theory, markets and competition, welfare, game theory, and adverse selection and moral hazard. The second half covers how the aggregate economy is measured, growth and development, economic fluctuations, stabilisation policy, money and inflation, unemployment, and financial and sovereign crises.

title: Research
text:
Paying to Be Paid Early: Debt Bondage in India’s Brick Kilns Paper


Abstract

Bonded workers take credit from their employer, and voluntarily forgo the freedom to leave until this is repaid. This paper asks why, using India’s brick kilns as a setting, to which 15 million workers migrate annually on advance payment contracts. The charge on the advance is not stated: it is built into a lower piece rate, and I test whether workers make mistakes when calculating it. Partnering with employers, I advertise real vacancies with randomised terms to 1,494 Odisha households. Workers favour high advances by 10 percentage points, implicitly borrowing at 19.5% per month. Demand concentrates amongst credit constrained workers and spikes after negative income shocks, as a rational borrower’s would. However, workers fail the arithmetic the trade-off requires, and three quarters wrongly believe high advance jobs pay more. Making the charge explicit in an information intervention fails to correct these deeply entrenched beliefs or dampen advance demand, suggesting regulation may be necessary to protect workers from costly mistakes.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers
Blossoming Towns (submitted) With Niclas Moneke and Céline Zipfel. Paper


Abstract

Towns and cities create jobs and income. Can the arrival of new jobs also create a town? We study large agro-industrial labour demand shocks in rural sub-Saharan Africa: flower farms in Kenya. Rising production costs in Europe generate a boom in Kenyan cut-flower export production, providing stable wage jobs for mostly low-skilled women. We exploit the specific requirements of cut-flower production to track the arrival and growth of greenhouses over the last two decades. We find large increases in wage employment and hozme-to-market transformation within agriculture, especially for women. Urbanisation unfolds: population growth and in-migration are flanked by an emerging private rental market for housing. Housing quality and infrastructure access improve, wealth accumulates. Educational investments increase while fertility decreases. Suggestive evidence highlights that the resulting towns initiate occupational change, motivate forward-looking investment and even survive flower farm closures – indicating towns that can sustain themselves as centres of economic activity.

title: Research
text:
Work in Progress
Jobs to End Poverty: Evidence from Bangladesh With Oriana Bandiera, Robin Burgess, Stefano Caria, Munshi Sulaiman and Jack Thiemel.


Abstract

Do the poor have high returns from trainable human capital? Can they afford to pay for it? And are they differentially targeted by the organizations that offer training? We provide unique evidence on these questions by combining a household census (N=42,895) in urban Bangladesh, a randomized controlled trial of an on-the-job training intervention, unique data on the targeting of the implementing partner, and a structural model. We find that take-up of the training at full price is minimal, and there are no effects on labor market outcomes. The poor, however, increase employment and consumption under a 70% discount. We also document that, for the same program, the implementing NGO would have selected richer beneficiaries who are more likely to enroll in training. Our structural model rationalizes these findings by estimating that the poor have higher-than-average returns to training, but they also experience higher participation costs, and are hence targeted less frequently by an implementer that wants to maximise take-up. We confirm the central finding that the poor have higher-than-average returns to training in a re-analysis of previous training experiments, using machine learning predictions of outcomes and treatment effects.

title: Research
text:
Publications
Distributional and Climate Implications of Policy Responses to the Energy Crisis: Lessons from the UK With Thiemo Fetzer and Ludovica Gazzè. Economic Policy, 2024, 39(120): 711–756. Paper Financial Times


Abstract

Which households are most affected by energy price shocks? How do interventions in energy markets affect these patterns? To investigate these questions, this paper introduces a measurement framework that leverages granular property-level data representing more than 50% of the English and Welsh housing stock. This framework will form the basis for current and future studies on the heterogeneous effects of the energy crisis more broadly. We find that the energy price shock has a more pronounced effect on relatively more affluent areas where energy use is higher at baseline. We document that commonly used untargeted interventions in energy markets significantly weaken market price signals for able-to-pay households. Alternative, more targeted policies are cheaper, easily implementable, and could better align energy-saving incentives.
